# AIRI — Architecture Walkthrough (screen-share notes)

For walking an interviewer through the actual code. Each section is
**directory → what to open → what to say**. Open the *smallest* file that makes
the point; do not scroll through large files on a share.

---

## Before you share your screen

```bash
uv run --frozen python examples/quick_demo.py
```

Run this first, in a terminal you keep visible. It drives one requirement through
the entire chain in a few seconds and prints real artifacts — so when you say
"the SQL is generated by Python", you can show the object rather than assert it.

---

## 0. The map (30 seconds, one screen)

```text
src/airi/
├── agents/requirement_parser/   natural language  → MetricIR        [LLM]
├── metric_ir/                   the contract + validation           [Python]
├── skills/                      domain knowledge × mechanism        [declarative]
├── tools/                       templates that emit SQL             [Python]
├── testing/                     automated metric checks             [Python]
├── experiments/                 datasets, labels, statistics        [Python]
├── reflection/                  evidence → hypotheses               [LLM, read-only]
├── refinement/                  bounded proposals                   [human-decided]
├── registry/                    versions, audit events, release     [governance]
├── production/                  adapters, identity, verification     [fail-closed]
├── temporal/                    PSI, OOT slice validation           [Python]
├── workflows/                   the pipelines that compose the above
└── api/                         FastAPI routers (116 operations)

airi-web/     Vue 3 UI — zero business computation
examples/     runnable demos, per-stage output
docs/         architecture, guides, history, interview material
```

**Say:** "Three colours. LLM does intent and interpretation. Python does every
artifact. Humans do every gate. Everything else in this tree is one of those."

---

## 1. The requirement parser — where the model is allowed to act

**Open:** `src/airi/agents/requirement_parser/parser.py` and `prompts.py`

**Say:** the model gets a prompt and must return a Pydantic model. Point at the
schema in `agents/requirement_parser/schemas.py` — that is the contract.

**The line to land:** "This is the *only* place the model produces anything
structurally meaningful, and it produces IR — not SQL. There is no code path in
this repository that accepts SQL text from a model."

---

## 2. Metric IR — the boundary

**Open:** `src/airi/metric_ir/models.py`

Show the fields, then show two things that make it a *real* boundary rather than
a data class:

- the identifier pattern (`^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,63}$`) — no hyphens, no free text
  where an identifier belongs;
- the optional extension fields: `joins`, `column_filters`, `source_alias`,
  `aggregation_alias`.

**Say:** "These four are optional and were added last. Because they are optional,
the schema version stayed `1.0.0` and this required **no database migration**.
Backward compatibility was a design input, not luck."

**Open:** `src/airi/metric_ir/joins.py`

**Say:** this is the entire join grammar — `INNER`/`LEFT` only, equality only.
Small on purpose. Every restriction here is a thing that cannot happen in
production.

**Open:** `src/airi/metric_ir/semantics.py`

**Say:** canonical hashing lives here. This is what makes the approval hash
meaningful — the hash has to cover everything that changes the SQL, *including
joins*. If it did not, you could change a join and reuse a stale approval.

---

## 3. Skills — domain vs. mechanism

**Open:** `src/airi/skills/capabilities.py` (short, worth showing in full), then
`src/airi/skills/invoice.py` and `src/airi/skills/enterprise_relation.py`

**Say:** capabilities are declared **once** and pinned to tool versions:

```text
metric_window      @1.0.0 → generate_spark_sql_metric @1.1.0
metric_sum         @1.0.0 → generate_spark_sql_metric @1.1.0
metric_count       @1.0.0 → generate_spark_sql_metric @1.1.0
metric_growth_rate @1.0.0 → generate_growth_rate_sql   @1.0.0
metric_join        @1.0.0 → generate_spark_sql_metric   @1.3.0
```

Then show that `invoice.py` and `enterprise_relation.py` are **the same shape** —
they differ in semantics and in which capabilities they reference. Both
scenarios are ~80 lines of declarative content.

**The strongest single sentence in the whole walkthrough:**
"The second scenario needed a two-hop join. I did not write an
`enterprise_relation` join tool — I promoted the mechanism to `metric_join` and
pinned it. That is why `New Scenario ≠ New Workflow`, and it is why the *files
that differ* between the two scenarios are only these two."

---

## 4. Tools — where SQL actually comes from

**Open:** `src/airi/tools/base.py` (the interface), then
`src/airi/tools/spark_sql.py`, then one template:
`src/airi/tools/templates/spark/join_metric.sql.j2`

**Say:** the tool renders a fixed template with validated IR values and returns
the SQL artifact plus its content hash. Look at how little the template varies —
that is the point. There is no branch in here that accepts model-authored SQL.

**Then open the join template specifically** (`join_metric.sql.j2`) — it is the
one that carries the second scenario, and it shows `COUNT DISTINCT` plus the
self-loop exclusion predicate.

---

## 5. Validation — the second line of defence

**Open:** `src/airi/workflows/development/validation.py` (the closed grammar) and
`src/airi/workflows/development/join_validation.py` (the join-specific grammar)

**Say:** "Even though Python wrote this SQL, it still has to pass. The validator
is deliberately a **closed grammar, not a general SQL parser and not a substring
check** — it full-matches the projection, the qualified source, two `DATE`
bounds and one group key, which rejects comments, nested queries, UDFs, `OR`,
`UNION`, extra statements and clauses by construction. Separately, DDL/DML verbs
are refused outright: only `SELECT` is allowed."

The comment at the top of `validation.py` says exactly this — worth showing,
because "closed grammar instead of a security regex" is a decision an
interviewer will recognise.

This is worth showing even though it is a second layer — it demonstrates that the
architecture assumes its own generator could be wrong.

---

## 6. Testing — because the IR is structured, the platform knows what to test

**Open:** `src/airi/testing/planning.py` and `src/airi/testing/relation.py`

**Say:** `planning.py` decides *which* checks apply to this metric. `relation.py`
is the join-specific probe set — and it contains the one that makes the case:
a **direct-join control** that verifies the two-hop result against an
independent one-hop formulation. Eight checks, four probes.

That control is the difference between "the SQL ran" and "the SQL is correct".

---

## 7. Experiment + reflection — facts vs. hypotheses

**Open:** `src/airi/evaluation/` (the statistics), then
`src/airi/reflection/models.py` and `src/airi/reflection/diagnostics.py`

**Say:** statistics are computed in Python and stored as facts. Reflection reads
the facts and writes **hypotheses** — a different model, a different table.
`diagnostics.py` shows the diagnostic rules being deterministic.

**The line to land:** "A reflection cannot change the metric. It can only produce
a proposal. That is enforced by the storage layout, not by a convention."

**Open:** `src/airi/refinement/transform.py`

**Say:** this is where a proposal would become a bounded candidate — and it
requires a human decision first.

---

## 8. Registry — governed versions

**Open:** `src/airi/registry/versioning.py` and `src/airi/registry/models.py`

**Say:** versions are immutable; there is an active pointer; rollback exists.
`models.py` holds both the state and the audit-event stream — which is why
**adding an audit event type touches two enums** (a real bug I hit; good thing to
volunteer, it is the kind of detail that reads as authentic).

---

## 9. Production — the honest part

**Open:** `src/airi/production/adapters.py`, then `gate.py`, then mention
`verification.py` and `identity.py`

**Say:** "These exist and are exercised at the boundary, but they are **not
verified against a real environment** — there was no cluster. So they default to
inert and fail closed. `PROTECTED_REQUIREMENTS` in `production/models.py` defines
the requirements that are never waivable — artifact integrity, metric version
identity, actor authentication."

**Land this:** "I would rather show you the boundary of what I verified than
imply a capability I never ran. That is also why the integration tests for Spark,
MySQL, production identity and telemetry report **skipped** rather than mocked
green."

---

## 10. Web — thin by design

**Open:** `airi-web/src/api/` and one page, e.g.
`airi-web/src/pages/ExperimentPage.vue`

**Say:** every KS / IV / lift number and every version state comes from the
backend. The frontend does zero business computation, and the browser never
talks to an LLM. Governance conflicts render the backend's `error_code` instead
of inventing a message.

That is a deliberate constraint: a UI that recomputes business logic becomes a
second, ungoverned implementation of the metric.

---

## Close (one line)

"And that is the whole design: the model understands and interprets, Python
produces and verifies every artifact, and a human approves every gate. If you
only remember one thing — the SQL that runs was never written by the model."
